reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: One of the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias, marked by strictly unilateral attacks of severe orbital, supraorbital or temporal pain
Attacks are short, roughly two to thirty minutes, but very frequent, often occurring more than five times a day
Each attack carries ipsilateral cranial autonomic features such as tearing, conjunctival redness, nasal congestion or rhinorrhoea, eyelid oedema, and ptosis or miosis
The defining feature is a complete and lasting response to therapeutic indometacin, which serves as both a diagnostic test and the treatment
Compared with cluster headache the attacks are shorter and more frequent, and there is often a female predominance rather than the male predominance of cluster
Distinguished from SUNCT/SUNA by its longer attack duration and by the absolute indometacin response
A supervised indometacin trial with gastroprotection is used to confirm the diagnosis, and neuroimaging should precede labelling the disorder as primary
The course may be episodic with remissions or chronic and unremitting
reference.pathophysiology: Paroxysmal hemicrania belongs to the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias, a group in which activation of the trigeminovascular system is coupled to a cranial parasympathetic reflex. Functional imaging implicates the posterior hypothalamus in generating attacks, while trigeminal-autonomic reflex activity relayed through the sphenopalatine ganglion drives the ipsilateral autonomic signs such as lacrimation and nasal congestion. Why the disorder shows its characteristic near-universal sensitivity to indometacin remains incompletely understood but may relate to the drug's effects on prostaglandin-mediated vascular tone and intracranial pressure.
additionalDifferentials: Symptomatic trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia from a pituitary or posterior fossa lesion
additionalInvestigations: A detailed headache diary recording attack duration, frequency and accompanying autonomic features
Supervised indometacin trial, with gastric protection, to confirm the absolute response
MRI brain with dedicated pituitary and cavernous sinus views to exclude a symptomatic cause
Observation and documentation of cranial autonomic signs during an attack
Review of analgesic history to exclude medication-overuse headache
redFlags: Incomplete or absent response to an adequate indometacin trial, prompting a search for a secondary cause
Focal neurological deficit, papilloedema or other signs suggesting a structural lesion
New or changed headache in an older patient or with systemic symptoms
Attacks that fail to fit the expected short-duration, high-frequency pattern
reference.prognosis: With an adequate indometacin trial most patients gain complete relief; the episodic form may remit for long periods, while the chronic form usually requires ongoing preventive therapy, and prolonged indometacin use needs monitoring for gastrointestinal and renal effects.
pitfalls: Not performing a formal indometacin trial and thereby missing a highly treatable diagnosis
Mislabelling the disorder as cluster headache because of the shared autonomic features
Omitting neuroimaging and overlooking a pituitary or posterior fossa lesion that mimics the syndrome
Continuing long-term indometacin without gastroprotection or renal surveillance
references: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3)
management: Treat with indometacin, which produces a complete and lasting response and serves as both the diagnostic test and the definitive therapy
Co-prescribe gastric protection with a proton-pump inhibitor during indometacin therapy
For patients intolerant of indometacin, trial alternatives such as other COX inhibitors, topiramate or verapamil
Exclude a symptomatic secondary cause with MRI brain including dedicated pituitary and cavernous sinus views
Titrate to the lowest effective indometacin dose and attempt periodic withdrawal in the episodic form to detect remission
Monitor for gastrointestinal and renal adverse effects during prolonged indometacin use
